title: "4.5 Routers and project structure"
description: "Split the API into routers by resource, choose resource-shaped URLs, and lay out the project so each file has one clear job."

::: {.lesson-meta}
Part 4 · Lesson 5 · About 45 minutes
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Analogy: departments in a shop"}
A small shop has one counter. A department store has departments (shoes, kitchen, books), each with its own staff, all under one roof and one entrance. Customers find things faster, and staff know exactly what's theirs.

A **router** is a department of your API: all the routes for one resource, in one file, with a shared address prefix. The app is the building that puts the departments together.
:::

## Theory

With every route in `app.py`, the file grows to thousands of lines and every change touches it. FastAPI's **`APIRouter`** is a group of routes that you define in its own module and later attach to the app with `app.include_router(...)`. A router can set a `prefix` (`/issues`) and `tags` (for the docs) once for all its routes.

### Resource-shaped URLs

**REST** (Representational State Transfer, more in lesson 4.14) is the dominant style for HTTP APIs. Its core habit: URLs name **resources** (nouns), and HTTP methods say what to do with them (verbs).

| Method and path | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `GET /issues` | list issues |
| `GET /issues/42` | one issue |
| `PUT /issues/42/saved` | mark issue 42 as saved (for me) |
| `DELETE /issues/42/saved` | unsave it |
| `POST /repos` | add a repository |
| `GET /users/me` | the signed-in user |

Not `/getIssues` or `/saveIssue?id=42`: the method already says "get" or "save".

### Atlas's layout

```text
src/atlas/
  config.py          settings (lesson 4.2)
  models.py          tables (Part 3, plus users in 4.6)
  storage.py         database queries shared by CLI and API (Part 3)
  security.py        hashing and tokens, no FastAPI imports (4.6, 4.7)
  github_oauth.py    GitHub sign-in (4.8)
  api/
    app.py           create_app: middleware, error handlers, routers
    deps.py          dependencies: settings, session, current user
    schemas.py       request and response shapes
    idempotency.py   safe retries (4.12)
    routes/
      auth.py        /auth/...
      users.py       /users/me...
      repos.py       /repos
      issues.py      /issues...
      search.py      /search
      notes.py       notes (4.16)
```

The rule behind it: **code that knows about HTTP lives in `api/`; code that doesn't, lives outside.** `security.py` and `storage.py` can be used by the CLI, the API and the background worker (Part 5) alike.

Why not a "services" layer and a "repositories" layer between routes and the database, as some templates have? For an app this size, each extra layer is a file to jump through that does little but pass arguments along. Atlas's routes call SQLAlchemy directly and share real logic through `storage.py`. If a rule grows complex, it moves into a deeper module then, not before.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TB
  APP[app.py<br/>create_app] --> AUTH[routes/auth.py]
  APP --> USERS[routes/users.py]
  APP --> REPOS[routes/repos.py]
  APP --> ISSUES[routes/issues.py]
  APP --> SEARCH[routes/search.py]
  AUTH & USERS & REPOS & ISSUES & SEARCH --> DEPS[deps.py]
  AUTH --> SEC[security.py]
  SEARCH --> ST[storage.py]
  DEPS --> SEC
```

## In the project

A router module, `src/atlas/api/routes/search.py` (lesson 4.10 fills in the query):

```python
"""Keyword search over an indexed codebase (the same query as `atlas find`)."""

from fastapi import APIRouter

router = APIRouter(prefix="/search", tags=["search"])


@router.get("", response_model=SearchPage)
def search(session: SessionDep, q: str, ...) -> SearchPage:
    ...
```

`@router.get("")` with `prefix="/search"` answers `GET /search`. Every module in `routes/` exposes a variable named `router`, so `create_app` attaches them in one loop:

```python
from atlas.api.routes import auth, issues, notes, repos, search, users

for module in (auth, users, repos, issues, notes, search):
    app.include_router(module.router)
```

Once all of Part 4 is in place, the OpenAPI document lists these paths:

```text
$ curl -s http://localhost:8000/openapi.json | python3 -c "import json,sys; print(sorted(json.load(sys.stdin)[\"paths\"]))"
['/auth/login', '/auth/logout', '/auth/refresh', '/auth/register', '/health', '/issues', '/issues/{issue_id}', '/issues/{issue_id}/notes', '/issues/{issue_id}/saved', '/notes/{note_id}', '/ready', '/repos', '/search', '/users/me', '/users/me/saved-issues']
```

(The GitHub sign-in routes are hidden from the docs with `include_in_schema=False`: they're browser redirects, not calls a client makes.)

## Common mistakes

- **Circular imports**: `routes/users.py` imports from `app.py`, which imports `routes/users.py`. Shared things go in `deps.py` or `schemas.py`, which import nothing from routes.
- **Verbs in URLs**: `/issues/42/save` with POST. Use the resource (`/issues/42/saved`) and let the method be the verb.
- **Thin pass-through layers** (`IssueService.get_issue` calling `IssueRepository.get_issue` calling `session.get`): three files, one line of logic.
- **Forgetting `include_router`**: the routes exist in the module but answer 404.
- **Inconsistent plurals**: `/issue/42` and `/repos`. Pick plural nouns everywhere.

## Check yourself

**1.** What does `prefix="/issues"` on a router do?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
It's prepended to every route in the router, so `@router.get("/{issue_id}")` answers `GET /issues/{issue_id}`. The prefix is written once instead of on every route.
:::

**2.** Why does `security.py` live outside `api/`?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
It knows nothing about HTTP: hashing a password or signing a token is the same for the CLI (`atlas make-admin`), the API and tests. Keeping it free of FastAPI imports lets every part of Atlas use it.
:::

**3.** Design the URL and method for "list the notes I wrote on issue 42".

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
`GET /issues/42/notes`: notes are a sub-resource of the issue, and GET reads. This is exactly what Atlas builds in lesson 4.16.
:::

## Exercise

Move the `/stats` route from lesson 4.4's exercise into `routes/stats.py` with its own router (`prefix="/stats"`, `tags=["operations"]`) and include it in `create_app`.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
```python
from fastapi import APIRouter
from sqlalchemy import func, select

from atlas.api.deps import SessionDep
from atlas.models import Chunk, Repo

router = APIRouter(prefix="/stats", tags=["operations"])


@router.get("")
def stats(session: SessionDep) -> dict[str, int]:
    repos = session.scalar(select(func.count()).select_from(Repo)) or 0
    chunks = session.scalar(select(func.count()).select_from(Chunk)) or 0
    return {"repos": repos, "chunks": chunks}
```
Then add `stats` to the import and the `for module in (...)` loop.
:::

## Stretch

Sketch REST URLs for Part 6's features: asking a question about a repository, listing past answers, and rating an answer as helpful. Which method does each use?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
One reasonable design: `POST /repos/{repo_id}/questions` (ask; creates a question and its answer), `GET /questions` (my past questions), `GET /questions/{id}` (one with its answer), `PUT /questions/{id}/rating` with `{"helpful": true}` (set my rating; idempotent). Part 6 builds its own version and explains its choices.
:::

## What changed in the project

New `src/atlas/api/routes/` package with one router per resource; `create_app` includes them. Commit: `refactor: Split the API into routers`.
